title: Take and read (Confessions 8.12)
hook: in the garden, a child's chant, Romans 13, and his long wavering ends
tomorrow: what did a mother and son touch at a window?

segments.voice: Ponticianus told a story, and Augustine was turned around to face his own stalling. Your line: why not now? Today he asks it out loud.

Somewhere a kid is singing the same line over and over, the way kids do, until the whole house knows it by heart. A garden in Milan. Augustine has thrown himself down under a fig tree, crying. How long, he says. Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why not this hour? Then, from a house nearby, a child's voice, a boy or a girl, he can't tell, chanting over and over: take up and read, take up and read.
screen: `THE SAME LINE, OVER AND OVER.` → `UNDER A FIG TREE.` → `WHY NOT THIS HOUR?`

segments.voice: Augustine stops crying and tries to think: do children sing those words in some game? He can't remember any. So he takes it as a command from God, to open the book and read the first passage he finds. He remembers that Antony, from yesterday's story, once heard a Gospel read aloud and took it as spoken to him. He hurries back to where Alypius is sitting, picks up the book of Paul's letters, and reads in silence the first lines his eyes fall on. In the King James, from Romans: "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He reads no further, he says. He doesn't need to. A light, like certainty, pours into his heart. Then the small, human ending, the one to tell a friend. Alypius asks to see it, and reads one line past where Augustine stopped: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye." He takes that one for himself. Two friends, one book, and each finds his own verse.
screen: `A CHILD'S CHANT, OVER AND OVER.` · `THE FIRST LINES HIS EYES FALL ON.` · `HE READS NO FURTHER.` · `ALYPIUS READS ONE LINE MORE.` · then, large: `TAKE UP AND READ.`

segments.voice: Open a Bible, on paper or on a screen, to any page, and read the first few lines your eyes fall on, out loud and slowly. Listen to how they sound in the room. Then sit with them for the rest of the time, without making them mean anything yet.
Take and read. A child's chant in a garden in Milan, a few lines of Romans, and the end of Augustine's long wavering.
Here's the line: take up and read; he read a few lines, and needed no more. Good night.

howItsDone: Some Christians read scripture slowly and prayerfully, a practice often called lectio divina; churches and teachers differ on opening the Bible at random, and Augustine's garden comes up when they talk about it.

fork.setup: your little brother hears this story and decides to open the Bible at random before every test, to see if he'll pass. what fits Augustine's garden?
options: great plan: the first verse tells you what will happen.
Augustine read to be changed, not to get a forecast.
the Bible should never, ever be opened at random.
fork.reveal: the chant sent him to read, and Romans spoke to how he would live. churches differ on opening at random, but it was never a forecast.

original.note: Latin: take up, read. the child's chant in Confessions 8.12.

trapdoor: what you thought: Augustine heard a voice boom from heaven.
what it means: a child's chant from a nearby house, take up and read, sent him to the first lines of Romans.
what a scholar hears: tolle lege; he links it to Antony, who heard a Gospel read and took it as spoken to him. he read Paul in Latin, not the English quoted here.
guess: a chant that sent Augustine to read Romans
a library rule for borrowing old books
a teacher's order to study for an exam

chat.says: stuck on the testimony. Pop said open his old bible and read whatever's there. isn't that kind of random?
options: Augustine did just that, and it met him. Not magic; just read what's there.
Totally random. A verse picked by chance can't mean anything to you.
Do it for every decision. The first verse you see is God's answer.
chat.meaning: Augustine took the chant as a call to open scripture and read. Churches differ on opening at random; reading what's there is the heart of it.

Milan.meaning: a city in northern Italy, where Augustine was living

Romans.meaning: Paul's letter to the Christians in Rome

chambering.meaning: an old King James word for sexual immorality

notes: Confessions lines are paraphrased (quoted: null); the Pusey (1838) wording was not checked word for word. 'Take up and read' is the carry; the Latin 'tolle lege' is in the original and trapdoor games.

Story beats from 8.12: under a fig tree, weeping; 'how long? to-morrow and to-morrow? why not now?'; a voice from a neighboring house, boy or girl unknown, chanting; he cannot recall any game with those words; Antony's hearing of the Gospel; the book of the apostle where Alypius sat; reads the first passage in silence; 'no further would I read; nor needed I'; light of certainty; Alypius reads on (Romans 14:1) and applies it to himself. Confirm each.
Romans 13:13 is quoted in full and 13:14 only to 'the Lord Jesus Christ' (the rest of the verse, about provision for the flesh, is left out for length).
Augustine read Romans in a Latin version; the KJV is quoted here as the public-domain English, and the trapdoor says so.
The hook places the garden in Milan, which the Confessions supports from 8.6–8.8; confirm.
howItsDone names lectio divina and says churches differ on opening the Bible at random; confirm.
